summary: Florida ties smoke alarm rules to building work, not to selling - nothing in state law makes a seller upgrade or prove alarms before closing.
alarmType: A one- or two-family home or townhome undergoing a repair or a 'level 1 alteration' under the Florida Building Code may use smoke alarms powered by a 10-year nonremovable, nonreplaceable battery instead of retrofitting alarms wired to the house. If a battery alarm is newly installed, or replaces an existing battery alarm, because of a level 1 alteration, its battery must be nonremovable, nonreplaceable and last at least 10 years. The 10-year battery rule does not apply to an alarm that is part of a centrally monitored or supervised system, uses low-power radio frequency wireless signalling, or has multiple sensors (such as a combined smoke and CO alarm) and is listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.
coAlarms: Separate statute, keyed to new construction. Every separate building or addition built on or after July 1, 2008 that has a fossil-fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace, an attached garage or anything else that gives off CO must have an approved working CO alarm within 10 feet of each sleeping room, or wherever else the Florida Building Code requires. A hardwired or battery CO alarm, or a hardwired or battery combination CO and smoke alarm, satisfies it. It does not reach existing buildings being altered or repaired unless the work is an addition (more floor area, stories or height). Cite: Fla. Stat. s 553.885, https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/553.885 - last amended 2010 (ch. 2010-176).
